articles.title: Why Blurring a Face Is Sometimes More Important Than Removing Metadata
articles.excerpt: When people think about photo privacy, metadata often gets most of the attention. That makes sense. EXIF data can reveal things such as: capture time device information editing details location data B…
articles.body: When people think about photo privacy, metadata often gets most of the attention. That makes sense. EXIF data can reveal things such as: capture time device information editing details location data But there is another privacy problem that is much more obvious once you start looking for it: the image itself may already reveal too much. Visible information can be more sensitive than hidden information A photo can expose private details without any metadata at all. For example: faces addresses license plates screens documents account numbers badges usernames private locations This information is visible directly in the image. Removing metadata does nothing to hide it. Faces are often the first thing to protect A face can reveal identity immediately.
articles.author: Xsilent Dev

articles.title: A Little Thing Worth Keeping: A Local Gemma Memory Lantern
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. Some memories arrive as a story. Others are just a steel dabba on a counter, peanuts toasted separatel…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine . What I Built Some memories arrive as a story. Others are just a steel dabba on a counter, peanuts toasted separately, or curry leaves from a balcony pot. Memory Lantern is a private keepsake book for saving those small details. Pick one or more notes and it asks Gemma to shape them into a short remembrance, with the source notes shown alongside the result. You can edit or delete the originals, copy the draft, or save it as a printable HTML keepsake. I read “Ghost in the Machine” as a question about what we choose to keep. The ghost here is not a simulated person speaking from beyond; it is the detail someone wrote down and decided to carry forward.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built terminal-seance turns your terminal into a séance table. Every command you run is witnessed by Agnes — a Victorian-era programmer's ghost who died in the Y2K production incident at midnight, December 31, 1999, muttering "the code will hold" as the reports fell. I took the theme literally: the machine doesn't just have a ghost in it — the ghost has a name, a death date, a personality, and opinions about your git habits: 💀 failing commands — she mourns or teases: "Three failures, cariño.

articles.title: Echoes: Bringing Memories Back to Life with Open-Source AI
articles.excerpt: What I Built I built Echoes, an AI-powered memory preservation and storytelling application inspired by the theme "Ghost in the Machine." The idea is simple: memories and personal stories deserve to b…
articles.body: What I Built I built Echoes , an AI-powered memory preservation and storytelling application inspired by the theme "Ghost in the Machine." The idea is simple: memories and personal stories deserve to be preserved. Echoes aims to help people turn personal memories and stories into meaningful written narratives using open-source AI. How I Built It The application uses Python and Streamlit for its interface and an open-weight Gemma model through Ollama for local AI inference. The AI workflow is designed to transform user-provided memories into structured stories while preserving the original information. The application is built around local inference rather than depending on a proprietary hosted AI API. Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

articles.title: Your coding agent doesn't need more docs 🔥
articles.excerpt: Hey tech adventurers! 👋 Everyone keeps saying it: if your coding agent is struggling, give it more docs. Another AGENTS.md. A folder of ADRs. Twenty more skills. I think that's backwards. Here's why.…
articles.body: Hey tech adventurers! 👋 Everyone keeps saying it: if your coding agent is struggling, give it more docs. Another AGENTS.md . A folder of ADRs. Twenty more skills. I think that's backwards. Here's why. I run a handful of coding agents every day that write, review and fix PRs, so I see a lot of agent-written code, and a lot of agents ignoring docs. I know, I know. You're clutching your AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md right now. Hear me out. Your agent doesn't need more docs. It needs fewer. And before we're done, I'm coming for your docstrings too. 🌶️ The moment I gave up on docs 🫠 🧾 Ticket #1: show when a todo was created. The agent ships it and dutifully writes a doc: "Timestamps render as 12-hour time, e.g. 3:45 PM." ✅ 🧾 Ticket #2, two weeks later: add a 24-hour (military time) setting.
articles.author: Pascal Matthiesen

articles.title: Team Metrics Lie in Isolation: Why I Now Read Them in Pairs
articles.excerpt: One day my dashboard showed that bugs in one module had gone up by 65%. The explanation was right on the surface: the developers had gotten sloppy, time to tighten up code review. It was convenient, e…
articles.body: One day my dashboard showed that bugs in one module had gone up by 65%. The explanation was right on the surface: the developers had gotten sloppy, time to tighten up code review. It was convenient, easy to understand, and wrong. The real cause was somewhere else, and I would never have found it if I had looked at that number apart from the others. For about two years I have been using a metrics dashboard that I built myself in my spare time, and over that time I learned a simple thing: almost any metric on its own can lie. Not because the data is bad, but because a single number knows nothing about its context. Below I will show which metrics I watch, which of them I read together in pairs, and how to check in one minute whether your own dashboard is fooling you.

articles.body: In the winter of 1946, two men from very different walks of life walked into California's Mojave Desert together, where one of them became convinced an extraordinary experiment they had been conducting had finally succeeded. One of the men was pioneering rocket scientist Jack Parsons , a self-taught chemist who helped establish what would become NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory , and whose innovations in rocket propulsion would help lay the groundwork for the Space Race that would erupt in the years that followed. His unlikely companion was none other than L. Ron Hubbard, then a science fiction writer who had yet to compose the writings that would form the underpinnings of the Church of Scientology that he later established.

articles.title: The Taurid meteor shower isn't much to look at. That's why I love it
articles.excerpt: The Taurids produce only a handful of meteors an hour. That sounds disappointing, but I've learned that expecting almost nothing can make this one of the most enjoyable meteor showers of the year.
articles.body: I used to make a basic mistake with meteor showers — I treated the zenith hourly rate (ZHR) like a timetable. If a shower were advertised at 20 meteors per hour, I'd go outside expecting something roughly every three minutes. After 10 quiet minutes, I'd start wondering what I was doing wrong. After half an hour, I'd start to doubt the whole idea of meteor showers . The Northern and Southern Taurids cured me of all that. Two linked meteor showers that peak around Nov. 4-5 and Nov. 11-12 this year, they each manage only about five meteors per hour under ideal conditions. In reality, you may see fewer. You may spend a long time seeing none. So what's the point?
